items.title: The Final Defenders
items.description: For the first time in her career, Cynthia Short let a folder of crime-scene photographs lie untouched on the corner of her desk, because she couldn’t bring herself to look at them. Short had been a criminal-defense attorney in Kansas City, Missouri, for 12 years, and on the payroll of the Missouri State Public Defender’s Office for the past decade. She had spent much of that time immersed in graphic records of the worst human conduct. Even so, the case of Richard DeLong had shocked her. DeLong, 34, was facing capital punishment for five counts of murder. In January 1999, he had killed his ex-girlfriend Erin Vanderhoef—who was shortly due to deliver their child, a daughter they had named Hannah—as well as the three school-age children she’d had with two other men. DeLong had entered their decaying clapboard house in Springfield, Missouri, on the morning of January 19 and strangled each member of the family using scarves and cords, hog-tying Erin and gagging two of the children. When he was arrested several days later, he promptly confessed to each of the murders and immediately became the most hated man in Springfield. Short wished she didn’t have to take the case, but it was her duty as a public defender. When, after several weeks, she finally forced herself to look at the crime-scene photos, she saw that the bodies of the children were partly hidden by debris—clothes, a plastic lawn chair, an overturned lamp. One of the boys, 10-year-old Chris, was still in bed; the other boy, 11-year-old Jimmy, had been left on the floor. Vanderhoef herself lay on her side on a rug in the living room, her blue top riding up over her pregnant belly. The youngest of the children, 8-year-old Darlene, was found in her sky-blue pajamas, tossed upside down onto a heap of garbage in the corner of her room, a jacket thrown over her face. Short was then raising two young children of her own, and she wasn’t sure she would be able to hide her revulsion from a jury. “As a public defender, I’d seen all sorts of things, but it was the first time where I thought, I don’t know that I can stand in the courtroom next to him ,” she told me when we first spoke by phone, in January. She also doubted that she could do much to help DeLong. He had committed a horrific crime and then admitted to it in a hateful taped confession. In capital trials in the United States, proceedings are typically split into two phases: The first phase establishes a defendant’s guilt or innocence; if a jury returns a guilty verdict, it then determines in the second phase whether the defendant is sentenced to death or to life in prison. Prosecutors sometimes agree not to pursue capital punishment in exchange for a guilty plea, and on Short’s advice, DeLong did offer to plead guilty and waive all appeals in exchange for life without parole. But the prosecutors had no interest in a deal. Because DeLong’s guilt was not in question, Short would focus on the sentencing phase. In capital cases, juries are instructed to consider statutorily defined aggravating factors cited by the prosecution—including, for instance, the death of multiple victims or of children, or the use of particularly sadistic methods of killing, all of which applied in DeLong’s case. Juries are told to weigh these aggravating factors against a much broader category of mitigating factors presented by the defense. These may include mental illness, intellectual disability, and a history of significant trauma or abuse. If the jury finds that the aggravators outweigh the mitigators, then it will likely hand down a penalty of death; if the mitigators prevail, then the jury will likely elect a lesser sentence, usually life in prison without parole. DeLong’s fate depended on Short’s ability to investigate his background and determine whether any possible mitigating evidence could be found that might persuade a jury to spare his life. Despite deep misgivings, Short threw herself into the case. She had inherited her work ethic from her father, who helped manage the Apollo program as NASA’s vice president of space operations. His job took the family all around the country, from New Jersey to California, Virginia to Texas. Both she and her husband were attorneys; she’d earned her degree at Saint Louis University School of Law. Short worked grueling hours, spending six days a week at the office and traveling so often that her children became accustomed to her absence. Once, Short startled her 5-year-old son when she arrived home early from a long work trip. Assuming that she had lost her case, he asked, “Is the man dead?” (Courtesy of Cynthia Short) When she took on Richard DeLong’s case, Short was raising two children of her own, and she wasn’t sure she’d be able to hide her revulsion from the jury. Short wasn’t opposed to the death penalty when she first started practicing law, but as she gained experience in capital cases, she came to doubt that the criminal legal system was capable of consistently producing fair and equal outcomes. Capital punishment is inherently arbitrary. Some defendants have money and seasoned legal teams at trial; others do not. Some prosecutors favor the death penalty and others don’t, meaning defendants might be executed not strictly because of the nature of their offense but because of the side of a state or county line on which they happened to commit it. As she came to understand the capriciousness of criminal justice, Short changed her mind about capital punishment. The experience of representing several defendants whom she believed had been wrongly accused strengthened her opposition. To defend Rick DeLong, Short knew, she didn’t need to make the jury believe that he was a good man or that he shouldn’t receive a terrible punishment. In capital trials in Missouri, as in most states, juries must return a unanimous verdict for a death sentence to be handed down, so Short needed only to introduce a shred of doubt in a single juror’s mind that her client had forfeited his right to live. But even that seemed daunting, given the repugnance that she, DeLong’s own lawyer, could not suppress. Short may have wished that she didn’t have to take this case, but it would ultimately change her perspective on criminal behavior and set her career on a new path, taking her from the public defender’s office to a field known as mitigation, then still developing but now a central feature of every legal defense in capital cases. Mitigators are investigators whose mission, now mandated by law and precedent, is the granular search for circumstances that might convince a jury that their clients deserve a lesser sentence; in their most crucial cases, these specialists are the final advocates for a defendant’s life. Short would help pioneer the field and become one of its foremost practitioners. But in January 1999, all she had was a guilty client and bad odds. Newspapers.com The front page of the Springfield News-Leader the day after Richard DeLong’s conviction D oubt is central to mitigation : creating doubt that a person is wholly given over to evil, or doubt that there is no universe—no set of terrible circumstances—in which you yourself might commit a horrific crime. I do believe that there are people who commit acts of perfect evil; a frank appraisal of human nature suggests as much. But those who oppose capital punishment, as I do, oppose the death penalty even for the worst criminals in the worst cases. The reason to stay the executioner’s hand has less to do with the nature of the defendant than it does with the nature of society: Showing mercy is morally beneficial to everyone. The legal system, of course, does not think this way; it needs a solid rationale to hang decisions on, and it must establish that what appears to be abject wickedness, and nothing else, may in fact be more complicated and tragic. The work of mitigation—searching for reasons a defendant’s life should be spared—is, unsurprisingly, not always well received in the legal community or by the public. As a society, we like to believe that our choices and actions are entirely within our control. Mitigators introduce an element of uncertainty. Their investigations routinely produce information that calls into question whether defendants would have, in better circumstances, committed their crimes at all. To some, this seems like making excuses for criminals. For Short, now 65, mitigation isn’t about rationalizing crimes. “It is about telling the truth,” she told me. “The crime is real. The harm is real. Nothing I do changes that.” She does not wish to downplay suffering or to pretend that something awful did not happen. The goal of a mitigator, she said, is to understand how a person becomes a criminal. “Every life leaves a trail. Abuse, neglect, poverty, brain injury, trauma, addiction, resilience, acts of kindness, moments of courage—all become a part of that person’s story,” Short told me over email. “Mitigation is not the art of making people less guilty. It is the discipline of making sure we judge them as a whole human being.” When Short was preparing for the DeLong case, mitigation had only just begun to emerge as a routine component of a legal defense in capital cases. It became formalized not long afterward, with the case of Kevin Wiggins. In September 1988, Wiggins, a Maryland construction worker, was charged with the murder of 77-year-old Florence Lacs. He had been arrested while driving her car and had already used her credit cards and pawned her jewelry. A jury convicted him of murder and sentenced him to death. But Wiggins, who was intellectually disabled and had been sexually abused as a child, appealed the sentence on the grounds that his attorneys had not presented sufficient evidence of extenuating circumstances in his defense. His case went to the Supreme Court, which ruled in his favor in Wiggins v. Smith in 2003. The Wiggins decision held that capital defendants have a right to an effective defense, including an investigation into circumstances that might explain their crimes—a ruling that fueled the rise of mitigation work. In 2008, the American Bar Association revised its guidelines to direct defense teams in capital cases to include both an investigator, who conducts an independent inquiry into the crime itself, and a mitigation specialist, who is responsible for producing information that might convince a jury that there is something more to a client than their crime suggests. Mitigators sift through the past and familiarize themselves with all elements of a defendant’s personal history. Fragments of clients’ lives may be strewn across the country or around the world, hidden among scattered documents and scattered memories. Mitigation specialists conduct scores of in-person interviews for each case—with extended family, friends, teachers, coaches, doctors, co-workers—to put the pieces together. The Marshall Project estimates that there may be fewer than 1,000 mitigation specialists nationwide; the majority of them deal with capital cases. About twice that number of people are currently on death row. Because mitigation specialists often have little time to prepare their cases for trial, they frequently continue their investigations during the long death-penalty appeals process. Legal teams involved in capital cases are typically reluctant to discuss their findings if judicial processes remain ongoing, but at the Mwalimu Center for Justice, a law office in New Orleans that handles capital appeals, mitigation specialists on staff agreed to share information they had uncovered about some of their clients. Benjamin Cole, an Oklahoma man who murdered his infant daughter a few days before Christmas 2002, was found by specialists on his defense team to be schizophrenic; a brain scan revealed a severe lesion. Cole spoke in riddles and frequently broke into song while interacting with his defense team, until his disease became so advanced that he chose to sit in his dark prison cell hoarding religious pamphlets and rotting food while his hair grew matted and his mind decomposed. The mitigators argued that he was too sick to be subject to execution under the Supreme Court’s 1986 decision in Ford v. Wainwright , but state authorities were undeterred. Oklahoma executed Cole in 2022. Sometimes mitigation, no matter how legitimate, cannot overcome people’s inherent disgust with horrific crimes. Cynthia Short was facing that very possibility. Sky Maggiore for The Atlantic Mitigators familiarize themselves with all elements of a defendant’s personal history. Sky Maggiore for The Atlantic Short worked on DeLong’s case throughout much of her third pregnancy. Short still hadn’t looked at the crime-scene photographs when she first met Rick DeLong, a few days after he was taken into custody in January 1999. But she had watched his maniacal taped confession, which would later be played at trial and shared with the Springfield News-Leader . “Now laugh,” he had reportedly said to 8-year-old Darlene Vanderhoef’s lifeless body as she lay thrown over a piece of bedroom furniture with an electrical cord around her neck. Even so, Short insisted on speaking with DeLong in person, with no partition between them and no shackles to hold him in place. He was much smaller than she had expected, thin and balding, and had a scraggly mullet and a dirty-blond beard. In Short’s experience, clients facing capital charges sometimes open a first conversation by declaring suicidal intent: The path ahead otherwise leads to either death in a prison cell or death in an execution chamber. But DeLong clearly wanted to live. And surprisingly, he was obsessed with the well-being of another person: Stacie Leffingwell, his long-term partner and the mother of his youngest child. Leffingwell had helped him kill Erin Vanderhoef and her children. And she was dying from AIDS. “Everything in that first conversation was what could I do for Stacie?” Short recalled. “How could I help Stacie?” In a photograph Short has seen, Leffingwell kneels next to DeLong and their infant son on a sunlit lawn, a mischievous smile flashing across her face. They had met in the early 1990s when DeLong was barbecuing in a friend’s backyard in Springfield and Leffingwell, a neighbor, dropped by and struck up a conversation. Leffingwell was dark-haired, petite, and funny. Born in California in 1967 to a teenage heroin addict, she had dropped out of high school and never learned to read. DeLong and Leffingwell both used drugs, especially methamphetamines. When they met, Leffingwell was HIV-positive, but she didn’t tell DeLong. He himself was the child of a teenage mother. Born in Springfield in 1964, he grew up in poverty and was subjected to vicious assaults by his stepfather. He began using drugs at the age of 15 and was eventually snorting or smoking meth several times a week. He got by on intermittent jobs as a mechanic and manual laborer. These details and more were revealed as Short worked with a mitigation specialist and former welfare caseworker named Kathy Schneider. The pair traveled six hours from Kansas City to Springfield and back each week to interview everyone they could find who knew DeLong. They interviewed people in parks and churches, and once went into a drug house in the middle of a snowstorm. Every month, Schneider went to see DeLong in jail, where she also interviewed his mother and sisters. Schneider created a history of DeLong’s family going back three generations, documenting the life of his biological father, a man known as Howard Littles, and his stepfather, Buzz, who had been diagnosed as mentally ill and institutionalized. DeLong was a twice-divorced father of four when, in 1996, he was introduced to Erin Vanderhoef, who worked at a McDonald’s in Springfield. Vanderhoef had also suffered a life marked by poverty and loss, and she took a liking to DeLong right away, confiding in others that she was interested in him romantically, even though he was already involved with Leffingwell. They formed a close friendship. DeLong had a child with Leffingwell, a son born in 1997 whom they named Lyle. Leffingwell had tried to stay clean during her pregnancy, but she resumed using drugs after the baby was born. She disappeared for a time, leaving DeLong alone to care for their newborn. Vanderhoef stepped in to help. When Leffingwell came home, she was in treatment for depression. DeLong and Vanderhoef by then were sleeping together. DeLong’s place was often in a state of chaos and frequented by drug users. Despite the infidelity and the strangeness of the arrangement, Leffingwell and Lyle moved in with Vanderhoef and her three children. A volatile love triangle developed. In February 1998, DeLong and Leffingwell abruptly moved into a motel in Joplin, roughly 70 miles west of Springfield, near the Kansas border. But DeLong still saw Vanderhoef, and by summer she knew she was pregnant. The news sent Leffingwell into a bout of jealousy and deeper into addiction. That July, she was admitted to a hospital for pancreatitis and stayed for three weeks. She weighed less than 90 pounds. Leffingwell and DeLong told family and friends that she had stomach cancer. In fact, she was dying of AIDS. In September, DeLong himself was diagnosed with HIV. He began using meth every day. In the days leading up to the murders, DeLong and Leffingwell went on a meth binge. On the night of January 18, 1999, Leffingwell was high and distraught, racked with fear that Vanderhoef was going to replace her. DeLong, for his part, was furious with Vanderhoef for messing up his relationship with Leffingwell. The couple came to the shared belief that Vanderhoef presented a problem, and Leffingwell demanded that DeLong fix it—permanently. Early the following morning, DeLong drove from Joplin to Springfield to kill Vanderhoef. Leffingwell rode with him, as did Harold “Bobby” Lingle, a friend and neighbor who had agreed to help carry out DeLong’s plan in exchange for an eight ball of meth. At around eight that morning, they pulled up to Vanderhoef’s three-bedroom house. Lingle, who had met Vanderhoef before, lured her out of the house on the pretext of a grocery errand so that DeLong and Leffingwell could wait and catch her by surprise when she returned. Then DeLong slipped inside, where he found Vanderhoef’s three children getting ready for school. Wired on meth, DeLong killed them one by one. When Vanderhoef came back, Lingle told her that the children had been sent to their rooms. Then he and Leffingwell helped DeLong subdue and murder Vanderhoef. It was a cold mercy that she died thinking her children were still alive. DeLong, Leffingwell, and Lingle were quickly apprehended. Leffingwell died of AIDS before the year was out. The lead Greene County prosecutor, Darrell Moore, decided not to seek the death penalty against Lingle, who was said to have an IQ of 72; he was eventually sentenced to life in prison without parole. But Moore was adamant about bringing capital charges against DeLong. A series of delays pushed DeLong’s trial to June 2001. Public furor in Springfield ran hot, and press coverage was intense. When Short stood before the jurors, the first thing she said was that DeLong was unquestionably guilty. She acknowledged the horror and disgust that they were surely feeling. “There are things that we need to do in this courtroom,” she recalled telling the jury. “And one of those things that you’re going to need to do is, you’re going to need to really look closely at his mental state. That will be your job.” But it would have to be a job mainly for phase two—the sentencing phase—rather than phase one, the guilt-or-innocence phase. No one was surprised when, on June 28, after a week and a half of testimony and less than four hours of deliberation, the jury convicted Rick DeLong on all five counts of murder. Sky Maggiore for The Atlantic “Mitigation is not the art of making people less guilty,” Short said. “It is the discipline of making sure we judge them as a whole human being.” Short knew that the sentencing phase would be difficult. She knew this in part because she had used her own extended family and friends—some of whom were highly conservative and generally skeptical of the defendants she represented—as test subjects, a kind of informal focus group. When Short and her team had finished their mitigation work, well before DeLong’s trial was scheduled to begin, they collated the findings into spiral-bound books, each more than 100 pages long. Inside were detailed descriptions of DeLong’s crimes, a DVD of his confession, photographs of the crime scene, and a photograph of Vanderhoef and her three children, young and bright and beautiful, posed on a bench in front of their mother, who is holding Lyle in her arms. The books also contained a detailed account of the mitigating factors in DeLong’s case, including his abusive stepfather, his drug addiction, and his HIV status. Scattered throughout were questionnaires asking readers for their reactions at various stages. The prompts had a clinical feel, as though Short were asking for opinions on a company’s new logo or a politician’s campaign slogan, not the killing of three children and a pregnant woman. If you did choose to look at the photographs, please describe what you learned from them . But it was the best simulation of a jury’s deliberation that Short could create. The responses from her family and friends were not encouraging. At the beginning of the book, readers were asked to gauge their support for capital punishment in general. One reader put her support at a 5 on a scale of 1 to 7, but after reading through the mitigation evidence, this same woman put her support for executing DeLong specifically at a 6. Her views were aligned with those of the prosecutor, Darrell Moore, who told reporters in advance of the sentencing phase that he and the judge had received numerous phone calls from angry citizens who wanted DeLong to die for his crimes. In front of the jury, Moore read a letter written by Vanderhoef’s brother in which he told DeLong, “You do not deserve the right to live, in a prison or any other place. You are not a man, you are a coward and an animal.” On DeLong’s behalf, Short introduced the array of mitigating information that she and Kathy Schneider had compiled. Some of the material had been presented in phase one—a tactic known as front-loading. The idea was not to try to sway jurors on the question of guilt or innocence—in this instance, there was nothing to be done—but to prepare the jury for arguments that would be presented again, and enhanced, later on. Short was aware that much of the information could be seen as all too familiar: When it comes to defendants facing the death penalty, a life like DeLong’s is normal; very few people guilty of aggravated first-degree murder have peaceful, healthy backgrounds. But two aspects of his story had taken Short by surprise. First, as she combed through the police files, Short had noticed a coincidence: Mark Deeds, the officer who had coaxed the confession out of DeLong and emerged as the hero of the investigation, had encountered her client before. In 1991, when DeLong was 27, he was arrested for selling cocaine and marijuana to Deeds, who was then working undercover for the Springfield Police Department. DeLong was so deeply enmeshed in the local drug culture that Deeds saw an opportunity. According to the testimony of DeLong’s former defense attorney, who negotiated a plea deal, Deeds threatened DeLong with decades in prison unless he began working as an informant. DeLong agreed. Police and prosecutors paid DeLong for information and granted him leniency on subsequent drug-related charges. At one point, his bond on arrest was reduced from $75,000 to $2,500. At another point, he received a sentence of five years’ probation for charges that ought to have resulted in prison time. The policies of the Missouri Board of Probation and Parole specifically prohibited offenders on probation from serving as police informants, but the department kept working with him anyway. Because of his protected status, DeLong continued to get little to no prison time when he was caught using. His addiction deepened. By the time of the murders, DeLong had helped Deeds and the Springfield Police Department clear a number of high-profile narcotics cases, even as he himself disintegrated from years of dependence. His career as a police informant came at the expense of any attempt at rehab—the one had simply precluded the other. Given all of this, Short asked, did the police bear any responsibility for DeLong’s condition? The second discovery that Short and her team made came while going through DeLong’s medical records. A week before the murders, he had begun taking Sustiva, an experimental drug that can help slow the progression of HIV but whose side effects include dizziness, insomnia, confusion, abnormal thinking, amnesia, agitation, and hallucinations. Patients abusing drugs or who have preexisting mental illness are at increased risk of developing neurological symptoms. And the drug’s side effects tend to be most severe when a patient is just starting to use the drug, as DeLong had been. The witnesses for the defense included an addiction specialist who testified that DeLong’s meth use easily could have contributed to a shattered mental state; a medical specialist who confirmed that Sustiva is known to induce delusions, hallucinations, and psychosis, and that the drug combined with meth could have disastrous results; and a psychiatrist who testified that DeLong had likely been in the grip of a psychotic episode when he carried out the murders. Short did not know what to expect when the jury began to deliberate. The new information had raised provocative questions about a case whose conclusion had once seemed preordained. In the end, the jury declined to impose the death penalty. It instead sentenced DeLong to life without parole. Sky Maggiore for The Atlantic In Short’s 23 years as a full-time mitigation specialist, she has worked with approximately 200 clients, none of whom has received the death penalty. Sky Maggiore for The Atlantic Cynthia Short in her home office in Kansas City, Missouri In 2003, Short left her job with the Public Defender’s Office due to a round of funding cuts, and decided to become a full-time mitigation specialist. In the 23 years since then, she says that she has worked with approximately 200 clients, none of whom has received the death penalty. Her attitude toward the field, as a practical matter, can be simply put: If mitigators are able to present a full picture of a defendant’s life, then no reasonable jury will return a verdict of death, not even for the most brutal killer. Her job is to persuade jurors to bestow something that she feels everyone deserves. “Mercy is not something that is earned,” she said to the jury during DeLong’s trial. “Mercy is something that is given.” Her words were printed in large display type in the Springfield News-Leader ’s front-page story about DeLong’s sentencing. Short is well aware that much of the public—including thoughtful citizens and community leaders—finds mitigation not only unjustifiable but incomprehensible. Still, she cannot set aside her principles or her obligations: Every defendant deserves a full measure of effort, even if onlookers deem it a waste of time and money for people who deserve nothing. She is sustained by some of those she encounters along the way. Several weeks after DeLong’s sentencing, Short received a note from James Spindler, the Greene County medical examiner. She had cross-examined him on the stand, and had probed him about his own struggles with drugs. Addiction, she suggested, was not something that happens strictly to evil and hopeless people. That resonated with Spindler, who wrote that although he had come across a number of dangerously antisocial defendants in his career whose executions he would by no means oppose, Short had convinced him that DeLong was not a “sociopath beyond redemption.” The past few years have been among the busiest in Short’s career as a mitigator. After a federal moratorium on new death sentences during the Biden administration—and the mass commutation of most federal death sentences already handed down—the Trump administration has reinstated the federal death penalty. Trump’s former attorney general Pam Bondi encouraged states to aggressively pursue capital punishment and take advantage of foreshortened appeals processes that would fast-track executions. Mitigation specialists have seen their workload increase in volume and urgency. Short’s determination to try to see beyond the worst of what her clients have done struck me as rare and admirable, and I kept it in mind when I picked up the phone to call the Missouri prison where Rick DeLong is incarcerated. I have spoken with many people who have committed murder, and many people on death row. Capital punishment, and the victims and perpetrators of capital crimes, have long been a focus of my reporting. But I had never spoken with a child killer before. A prison receptionist answered, and after a pause put DeLong on the phone. His voice was both hoarse and soft; his disease is advanced now, and he has had several heart attacks. He told me what his life had been like before he committed the murders, how he loved working as a mechanic—“There was nothing I couldn’t do to a car,” he said. He recalled his stepfather, and how abusive he was, and how the meth had made the bad moments more bearable. Meeting Leffingwell had made things better, too, because she came from the same world, and for once he felt understood. They had loved going to rodeos and carnivals together, a kind of fantastic escape. DeLong talked about his five children, only three of whom will speak with him. He also talked about his grandchildren, though he has seen them only in photos. His son Lyle is in prison, convicted of murder in 2022 and now serving a 32-year sentence. DeLong told me he had loved being a father to Lyle—“That’s my joy,” he said. “I took him everywhere.” He recalled bringing him on fishing trips, and once, in a misguided display of devotion, buying a heavy-duty backpack, cutting holes in it for arms and legs—a makeshift infant carrier—and taking him for rides on his motorcycle. Now the boy was a man, and had followed his father behind bars. As for his own crimes, DeLong told me that he was glad he’d been caught, and that he knows he deserves the sentence he received. I could not forget that the thin voice on the other end of the line belonged to a man who had taken five lives. It was also the voice of a frail 61-year-old slowly dying in prison. DeLong remembered Cynthia Short fondly, though he told me that he had initially doubted that a woman would be able to see past what he had done to a mother and her children. But Short, he admitted, had understood everything: the crime, his life, how he might appear in the eyes of a jury. And she knew what it would take to save him. He didn’t have much of a life anymore, but thanks to this woman, he was alive. “You couldn’t ask for better,” he told me. “There’s no way.”

items.title: Islamabad ATC summons Islamabad police chief in security breach case against Imaan and Hadi
items.description: ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Saturday summoned the Islamabad police chief and issued show-cause notices to two police officials over the continued failure to produce the case record in the security breach case against lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her spouse, Hadi Ali Chattha. The case pertains to the alleged disruption of a security route of an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. Imaan and her husband were accused of removing barriers from the route. The couple was indicted in the case on Oct 7. During Saturday’s hearing, ATC Judge Abul Hasnat Muhammad Zulqarnain directed the two police officials to whom notices were issued to explain their failure to ensure the production of the record. He warned that they could face imprisonment if it was not presented before the court. During the proceedings, the court expressed displeasure over the continued absence of the investigating officer and raised questions about the whereabouts of the case record. A court official informed the judge that the investigating officer had travelled to Gilgit-Baltistan and had not returned. The judge immediately summoned the superintendent (investigation) to explain the situation. Advocate Riasat Ali Azad, representing the accused, told the court that the bail application had been filed on October 29 last year and notices had already been issued, but the proceedings could not move forward because the investigating officer failed to appear with the record. He argued that in similar cases, another police official usually appeared with the case record when the investigating officer was unavailable. Questioning how long the court was expected to wait, Azad urged the judge to make a decision in accordance with the law. Advocate Asif Irfan, vice chairman of the Islamabad Bar Council, observed that the court was not powerless, but had so far been unable to ensure the production of the record. Advocate Aleem Abbasi, meanwhile, urged the judge to exercise his authority and decide the matter on merit. He added that the legal fraternity stood with the judiciary in defending its independence, but questioned how lawyers could secure justice for their own children if the judicial system failed to deliver it. Advocate Zafar Khokhar also questioned under which law an investigating officer could take the case record away and leave court proceedings stalled. Judge Zulqarnain, however, expressed displeasure over the tone adopted by some lawyers, deeming such conduct inappropriate and remarking that he was not influenced by vlogs or commentary and always conducted proceedings impartially. After a short break in the proceedings, SP Khurram Ashraf and Deputy Superintendent (DSP) Naeem Yousuf appeared before the court. The SP informed the judge that the investigating officer had travelled to Khaplu and would appear after he returned. The judge questioned the arrangement and asked when the officer would return, observing that everyone was waiting while the court had a case to decide. When pressed for a definite timeline, DSP Yousuf said the investigating officer could take another 10 to 15 days to return. The judge criticised the police for causing prolonged hardship to PTI workers through delays in their cases. Expressing frustration over the situation and the alleged harassment of workers, the judge ordered the discharge of several individuals arrested in connection with the PTI’s long march. The court subsequently issued show-cause notices to the SP and DSP, warning that failure to produce the case record could lead to proceedings for their imprisonment. Islamabad Inspector General of Police Muhammad Sohail Chaudhry was also summoned for the next hearing on November 3. The case The lawyer couple has been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) in a case pertaining to controversial social media posts. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On Sept 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the Supreme Court suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the IHC’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand. The fresh case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio. Imaan and Hadi were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added. The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties). They were indicted in the case on Oct 7 and the ATC on Oct 10 disposed of the couple’s petition seeking to drop the terrorism charges. On Oct 15, the court directed lawyers and witnesses in the case to appear at Adiala jail for the next hearing after police cited difficulties in transporting the couple to court. At yesterday’s hearing, Imaan and Hadi had objected to the manner in which they were presented during the hearing of the case, with the couple and their lawyers eventually walking out of the proceedings at Adiala jail.

Deputy Finance Minister calls for stronger internal controls to protect public funds
items.description: Deputy Minister for Finance, Thomas Nyarko Ampem, has called for stronger internal controls across public institutions to prevent financial irregularities and safeguard public funds. He said effective internal auditing was critical to ensuring that public resources were properly managed and channelled into development priorities under the government’s New Economy agenda. Speaking at the 25th anniversary of the Institute of Internal Auditors Ghana, Mr Ampem said internal auditors must move beyond identifying weaknesses after they had occurred to helping institutions prevent financial losses. He said Ghana’s development ambitions required significant investments in infrastructure, skills, technology and productive enterprises, making it imperative to protect limited public resources from waste and financial mismanagement. “Our ambition is to build a more productive, industrialised and resilient economy that creates jobs, adds value to our resources and improves livelihoods,” he said. “But we cannot mobilise scarce resources for development on one hand and allow them to leak through weak financial controls on the other.” Mr Ampem, who spoke on behalf of the Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, cited figures from the 2025 Auditor-General’s reports showing that financial irregularities across five categories of public institutions declined from approximately GH¢20.72 billion in 2024 to GH¢7.69 billion in 2025, representing a 62.9 per cent reduction. He welcomed the decline but said the remaining irregularities demonstrated the need for sustained efforts to strengthen accountability and improve public financial management. “A 62.9% reduction is progress. GH¢7.69 billion in remaining irregularities is a reminder that the job is far from finished,” he said. The Deputy Minister also highlighted findings from the audit of the government’s legacy arrears and payables, which saw GH¢8.1 billion out of GH¢68.7 billion in claims submitted for verification rejected. He said the rejected claims included those with inadequate supporting documentation, duplicate claims, falsified receipts and claims for work not done. “The lesson is that it is better to stop an improper payment before it is paid than to spend years trying to recover it,” he said. Mr Ampem urged internal auditors to strengthen their scrutiny of procurement processes, payroll systems and major public investments to identify risks early and prevent the misuse of public funds. He called for the adoption of data analytics, digital tools and continuous risk assessment, stressing that digitalisation must be supported by professional competence, institutional independence and management accountability. He also urged heads of institutions to empower internal auditors, protect their independence and act promptly on audit recommendations rather than allow the same weaknesses to recur. The success of the government’s New Economy agenda, he noted, would depend not only on the resources mobilised but also on how effectively they were safeguarded and utilised. “We cannot build a New Economy with old habits of waste, weak controls and avoidable financial losses,” he said.

items.title: Social engineering, not hacking, driving MoMo fraud in Ghana – MobileMoney Fintech LTD
items.description: Mobile money fraudsters in Ghana are increasingly exploiting human behaviour rather than relying on sophisticated hacking techniques to steal customers’ money, according to MobileMoney Fintech LTD’s Senior Manager for Financial Crimes, Moses Tetteh. He said fraudsters were using social engineering tactics to manipulate unsuspecting users into disclosing sensitive information, which they then use to access mobile money wallets and banking applications. Mr Tetteh made the remarks in an interview with MyJoyOnline on the sidelines of the 15th Absa-UPSA Law School Quarterly Banking Roundtable at the Absa Head Office in Accra. The forum brought together banking, legal and fintech experts to discuss emerging financial crimes and challenges facing the financial services sector. “Here, what the fraudsters may do is call the customer. And when they call the customer, they use either trust, fear, or a story to bring out greed. And then, once the customer falls for it, they’re able to take the customer’s credentials,” he said. He explained that once fraudsters obtain a victim’s login details, PIN or other authentication information, they can use them to access digital platforms and transfer funds. Mr Tetteh said the growing threat required greater vigilance from both customers and mobile money agents, who play a frontline role in facilitating transactions. “We are advising our customers to be more vigilant, and the same warning goes to our agents,” he cautioned. He said the fight against fraud should not be left to telecommunications companies and service providers alone, but should involve every participant in the digital financial ecosystem. “For us, we see the fight against fraud as a shared responsibility. Shared responsibility means that you do not just leave it to the service provider, the telcos alone, but collectively, we, as operators, and the customer, as the user, come together to fight against fraud,” he said. According to him, protecting access credentials is one of the most effective ways customers can reduce their exposure to fraud. “The first line of defence when it comes to any security system is access control, which is in the hands of the customer. So, as much as possible, if we limit the breach of credentials, then we would be able to mitigate some of these kinds of cases that we continue to record,” he added. The discussion at the roundtable also examined whether warnings about one-time passwords (OTPs) were sufficient to protect customers from fraud. Mr Tetteh said OTPs were only one of several sensitive credentials users needed to keep confidential. “So, OTP is one of the many credentials that, as a customer, you would have to keep secret. And if we say OTP, that’s the one-time password. You may have your PIN as well, which we expect you not to share either,” he said. He further warned customers against sharing private links used to facilitate the download of the MoMo application, stressing that such information should not be disclosed to third parties, including people claiming to be company staff. “That link is supposed to be kept private. He advised customers not to share that with any third party, not even MTN workers, because it is personal to you,” he said. Mr Tetteh said MobileMoney Fintech LTD continued to invest in customer education to remind users of the need to protect their credentials. The company also conducts periodic training for mobile money agents to improve their security awareness and professionalism in handling transactions. He said agents were taught to remain alert to their surroundings and ensure that sensitive customer information disclosed during transactions was not exposed to bystanders. The training, he explained, was intended to make agents more conscious of their environment and the risks associated with handling customers’ confidential information. Mr Tetteh urged customers who suspect that their information may have been compromised during a transaction to report the matter promptly, particularly if they begin receiving suspicious calls shortly afterwards. He said early reporting could help operators investigate suspected breaches and take steps to limit further exposure.

items.title: Dubréka-Télimélé : 105 kilomètres d’enfer pour les usagers de cet axe
items.description: Sur l’axe reliant Dubréka à Télimélé, la chaussée dégradée met à rude épreuve les voyageurs et les transporteurs. Entre nids-de-poule, portions détériorées et risques de panne, les usagers dénoncent des conditions de circulation difficiles et appellent l’État à intervenir. Il suffit de franchir le barrage de Souapiti pour mesurer l’ampleur des difficultés. Sur la route reliant Dubréka à Télimélé, la circulation se transforme en une épreuve de patience et d’endurance. Sur environ 105 kilomètres, les nids-de-poule et les portions fortement dégradées obligent les véhicules à avancer au ralenti. Rouler au pas, par nécessité Au volant, impossible de relâcher sa vigilance. Les chauffeurs ralentissent, scrutent la chaussée et tentent d’éviter les parties les plus abîmées. À l’arrière, les passagers subissent les secousses et la fatigue, sans pouvoir prévoir avec précision leur heure d’arrivée. Sur ce tronçon, ce n’est pas seulement la distance qui épuise les voyageurs, mais surtout l’état de la route. Mamadou Yansané, chauffeur, en fait l’expérience au quotidien. Selon lui, la fin de la saison des pluies ne facilite guère les déplacements. « Ce trajet nous crée suffisamment de problèmes sur la fin de cette saison des pluies », confie-t-il. Un constat partagé par de nombreux usagers contraints de composer avec une chaussée dégradée, au détriment de leur confort et de la durée de vie de leurs véhicules. Les transporteurs paient le prix fort Pour les transporteurs qui empruntent régulièrement cet axe, les conséquences sont multiples : risques de panne, usure prématurée des véhicules, dépenses supplémentaires d’entretien et allongement du temps de parcours. Autant de contraintes susceptibles de peser sur leurs revenus et sur le coût du transport des personnes et des marchandises. Pour beaucoup d’usagers, le choix de cet itinéraire relève davantage de la nécessité que du confort. Un autre voyageur explique que la route reliant Télimélé à Kindia est encore plus difficile à emprunter. « La route Télimélé-Kindia est impraticable, c’est pourquoi nous empruntons cette voie. L’État doit nous aider », lance-t-il. Faute d’alternative satisfaisante, les voyageurs se retrouvent ainsi contraints d’emprunter un axe lui-même fortement dégradé. Leur appel s’adresse directement aux autorités, auxquelles ils demandent une intervention pour améliorer les conditions de circulation. Un isolement qui pèse sur le quotidien Pour les habitants de Télimélé et des localités environnantes, les difficultés ne se limitent pas au trajet. Les déplacements vers les autres centres urbains, les marchés et les services essentiels deviennent plus contraignants. L’état des routes joue un rôle déterminant dans les échanges commerciaux et la mobilité des populations. Lorsqu’un axe est dégradé, les déplacements prennent davantage de temps, les coûts augmentent et les activités économiques peuvent en pâtir. Pour les communautés qui dépendent de cette liaison routière, la réhabilitation de la chaussée représente donc un enjeu qui dépasse le simple confort des voyageurs. Les usagers interpellent l’État Face à cette situation, les usagers souhaitent une intervention des pouvoirs publics pour améliorer la praticabilité de cet axe. Une évaluation de l’état de la chaussée, suivie de travaux d’entretien ou de réhabilitation adaptés, pourrait contribuer à réduire les difficultés rencontrées par les automobilistes et les transporteurs. Combien de temps faudra-t-il encore pour relier Dubréka à Télimélé dans des conditions acceptables de sécurité et de confort ? Pour les populations riveraines et les voyageurs, disposer d’une route praticable n’est pas un privilège, mais une nécessité. La mobilité, les échanges commerciaux et le développement local en dépendent.

items.title: ONU : Macky Sall retire sa candidature au poste de secrétaire général
items.description: Senegal's President Macky Sall arrives for the closing session of the New Global Financial Pact Summit, on June 23, 2023 in Paris. (Photo by Lewis Joly / POOL / AFP) " data-large-file="https://i0.wp.com/mediaguinee.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/IMG_0926.jpeg?fit=1024%2C682&ssl=1" /> L’ancien président sénégalais Macky Sall a annoncé, samedi 17 octobre 2026, le retrait de sa candidature au poste de secrétaire général des Nations unies. Dans une déclaration publiée à Marrakech, il évoque sa volonté de favoriser une candidature consensuelle, tout en réaffirmant son engagement en faveur de la paix, de la coopération internationale et d’une meilleure représentation de l’Afrique dans la gouvernance mondiale. C’est la fin de la course de Macky Sall au poste de secrétaire général de l’Organisation des Nations unies (ONU). L’ancien chef de l’État sénégalais a décidé de retirer sa candidature à l’issue du vote informel du Conseil de sécurité du 16 octobre 2026, après des consultations avec les présidents du Burundi et du Sénégal. « J’ai décidé de retirer ma candidature audit poste », annonce-t-il dans sa déclaration datée du 17 octobre à Marrakech. Cette décision, explique-t-il, répond à un « profond sens des responsabilités », avec l’espoir de contribuer à l’émergence d’un candidat susceptible de recueillir un consensus au sein du Conseil de sécurité. Une préférence pour l’Amérique latine et les Caraïbes Pour justifier son retrait, Macky Sall se réfère aux résultats des différents votes informels organisés depuis le début du processus de sélection du prochain secrétaire général de l’ONU. Selon lui, « les résultats des différents votes tests indiquent un choix en faveur d’une candidature issue de la région d’Amérique latine et des Caraïbes, et éventuellement féminine ». L’ancien président sénégalais remercie les dirigeants qui ont accompagné sa démarche, notamment Évariste Ndayishimiye, président du Burundi et président en exercice de l’Union africaine, qui a parrainé sa candidature, ainsi que Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye, président du Sénégal et président en exercice de la CEDEAO, qui l’a soutenue. Il adresse également ses remerciements aux États membres du Conseil de sécurité ayant voté en sa faveur, à son équipe de campagne et aux autorités religieuses et coutumières. Il salue aussi le soutien des Sénégalais, des organisations politiques et de la société civile, ainsi que de ses amis en Afrique et à l’étranger. Près de 40 ans d’expérience au service de l’ONU Macky Sall affirme que sa candidature était avant tout motivée par sa volonté de mettre son expérience au service de l’organisation internationale. « Ma candidature était essentiellement motivée par la volonté de mettre mon expérience de près de quarante ans de vie publique au service des Nations Unies », souligne-t-il. Malgré son retrait, l’ancien dirigeant entend poursuivre son engagement en faveur des idéaux qui ont guidé sa démarche. Il estime que l’organisation internationale doit évoluer face aux crises qui secouent le monde. « Les Nations Unies doivent engager une transformation profonde de leurs méthodes de travail et de leur fonctionnement », déclare-t-il, évoquant la multiplication des conflits, l’aggravation des rivalités géopolitiques, la fragmentation de l’ordre international et des défis économiques et financiers sans précédent. L’Afrique appelée à renforcer sa place dans la gouvernance mondiale Au-delà de sa candidature, Macky Sall insiste sur la nécessité pour le continent africain de peser davantage dans les décisions internationales. « L’Afrique, qui est au cœur des enjeux de paix, de sécurité et de développement, doit aussi continuer à faire entendre sa voix et poursuivre ses efforts afin d’occuper la place qui lui revient dans la gouvernance mondiale », affirme-t-il. L’ancien président sénégalais conclut sa déclaration en réaffirmant son attachement à la paix, à la sécurité, au développement économique et social, à la coopération internationale et au dialogue entre les nations. « Je retire ma candidature, mais reste pleinement engagé au service des idéaux qui l’ont inspirée », insiste-t-il, avant de souhaiter « plein succès à la personne qui sera appelée à exercer les hautes responsabilités de Secrétaire général des Nations Unies ». Son retrait ouvre ainsi la voie à la poursuite du processus de sélection du successeur d’António Guterres à la tête de l’organisation mondiale. Christine Finda KAMANO L’article ONU : Macky Sall retire sa candidature au poste de secrétaire général est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Région des Koulsé : Le Premier ministre lance le Pacte Nekré pour refonder l’école burkinabè
items.description: Le Burkina Faso franchit une nouvelle étape dans le processus de refondation de son système éducatif. Le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a présidé, ce samedi 17 octobre 2026 à Kaya, dans la région des Koulsé, la cérémonie officielle de lancement du « Pacte Nekré » pour la refondation de l’éducation burkinabè. La cérémonie s’est tenue sous le haut patronage du Président du Faso, chef de l’État, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré. À travers cette initiative, les autorités burkinabè entendent engager une transformation profonde de l’école nationale, avec pour ambition de former des citoyens responsables, engagés et utiles au développement du pays, au-delà de la seule acquisition de diplômes. Le Pacte Nekré se veut ainsi un référentiel destiné à orienter les changements nécessaires pour adapter le système éducatif aux réalités et aux besoins du Burkina Faso. Cette refondation prévoit notamment une adaptation des programmes scolaires aux besoins du pays, à travers la révision des curricula et des supports pédagogiques. Elle entend également renforcer la prise en compte des réalités socioculturelles nationales dans les apprentissages, tout en accordant une place plus importante aux savoirs endogènes, aux travaux manuels et à l’initiation aux métiers. La formation civique et patriotique figure également parmi les orientations de cette démarche. L’objectif est de contribuer à former des citoyens responsables et engagés, capables de participer activement à la construction nationale. À travers le Pacte Nekré, les autorités ambitionnent de faire de l’éducation un levier majeur du développement du Burkina Faso, en l’inscrivant dans une dynamique de transformation et de valorisation des ressources humaines nationales. Au cours de la cérémonie, le Pacte Nekré a fait l’objet d’une remise symbolique aux gouverneurs des régions, en vue de son appropriation au niveau territorial. Plus de détails à venir sur Minute.bf.

Le rassemblement a commencé au milieu de la matinée devant le siège de l’Union générale tunisienne du travail (UGTT), place Mohamed Ali, au centre-ville de la capitale, et la foule des manifestants a grossi au fil des heures et s’est rassemblée devant le théâtre municipal de Tunis. items.title: Guinée: l’organisation et le fonctionnement du Service national des infrastructures judiciaires et pénitentiaires, définis
items.description: Par un décret rendu public ce vendredi 17 octobre, Le président de la République a défini le mode d’organisation et de fonctionnement du Service national des infrastructures judiciaires et pénitentiaires. Cette structure est chargée de piloter les projets de construction, de rénovation, de réhabilitation et d’équipement des infrastructures du secteur de la justice. Doté d’un niveau hiérarchique équivalent à celui d’une direction de l’administration centrale, ce service aura pour mission principale d’élaborer et de mettre en œuvre les stratégies et programmes relatifs aux infrastructures judiciaires et pénitentiaires. Il assurera également le suivi de l’exécution des travaux. Parmi ses attributions figurent le contrôle du respect des normes techniques, environnementales et sociales, la garantie de la qualité des ouvrages, le respect des délais d’exécution et la maîtrise des coûts. Il sera aussi chargé de recenser et de préserver le patrimoine bâti et non bâti du ministère de la Justice et des Droits de l’Homme. Une direction appuyée par deux départements techniques Selon le décret, le service sera dirigé par un directeur nommé par décret, sur proposition du ministre de la Justice et des Droits de l’Homme. Il sera assisté d’un directeur adjoint, désigné dans les mêmes conditions. Son organisation comprendra un service d’appui chargé des affaires financières et deux départements techniques : celui des études et de la planification, et celui des travaux et du suivi. Le département des études et de la planification sera notamment chargé de réaliser les études de faisabilité, les études architecturales et techniques, ainsi que d’élaborer les normes de construction. De son côté, le département des travaux et du suivi assurera le suivi des chantiers de construction, de rénovation et de maintenance. Il sera également responsable de l’évaluation des projets et du suivi des équipements destinés aux infrastructures judiciaires et pénitentiaires. Des antennes régionales prévues Le texte prévoit par ailleurs la mise en place d’antennes régionales afin de renforcer la présence du service sur le terrain. Le personnel sera composé de fonctionnaires et d’agents contractuels de droit public. La structure pourra également bénéficier de financements provenant de partenaires techniques et financiers. Ces ressources seront versées dans un compte spécial ou inscrites dans un budget annexe. Enfin, les chefs de département seront nommés par arrêté. Les chefs de cellules et les responsables des antennes régionales seront, quant à eux, désignés par décision du ministre de la Justice et des Droits de l’Homme, sur proposition du directeur du service.

Recrutement de 6 000 enseignants : forte mobilisation des candidats à Kindia
items.description: Les épreuves du concours de recrutement de 6 000 agents pour le secteur de l’enseignement ont été officiellement lancées en République de Guinée. Dans la préfecture de Kindia, près de 14 000 candidats prennent part aux épreuves, répartis dans 31 centres. a cérémonie officielle de lancement s’est déroulée au collège Tafory, sous la présidence du secrétaire général du ministère de la Modernisation de l’Administration et de la Fonction publique. À l’occasion de cette cérémonie, le représentant du ministère a exprimé sa satisfaction quant à la forte mobilisation des candidats à Kindia, tout en saluant la tenue du concours à l’intérieur du pays. « C’est un sentiment de satisfaction qui m’anime ce matin en venant à Kindia, qui reçoit le plus grand nombre de candidats. Cela traduit toute la vision du président de la République, Son Excellence Mamadi Doumbouya, celle de permettre à notre ministère d’organiser le concours à l’intérieur du pays. Dans les sept régions, les concours se déroulent. Sur les 39 000 candidats pour 6 000 postes d’enseignants, près de 14 000 sont à Kindia. Il est donc important de venir visiter quelques centres et de voir comment les choses se passent. Dans les différentes salles, j’ai été particulièrement marqué par la forte participation des femmes. Cela traduit également la vision du président de la République, celle de dédier son mandat aux femmes. Nous sommes venus leur souhaiter bonne chance et constater que les épreuves sont bien distribuées et que toutes les dispositions sécuritaires sont prises. C’est aussi l’occasion de remercier les autorités locales et toutes les personnes mobilisées pour que ces épreuves se déroulent dans les meilleures conditions », a déclaré N’Faly Sylla, secrétaire général du ministère de la Modernisation de l’Administration et de la Fonction publique. Les autorités entendent faire de ce concours un processus transparent, avec une politique de tolérance zéro face à la fraude et à la corruption. À cet effet, un dispositif de signalement a été mis en place en collaboration avec l’Agence nationale de sécurité des systèmes d’information « On veut une tolérance zéro face à la fraude. Nous avons mis en place un dispositif avec le numéro 1017 pour permettre de signaler les cas de fraude, en collaboration avec l’Agence nationale de sécurité des systèmes d’information. Pour tout signalement, nous invitons les citoyens à se rendre sur la plateforme Alerte.gov.gn ou à appeler le numéro indiqué. Les cas seront recensés et transmis aux autorités compétentes afin que les mesures nécessaires soient prises », a précisé l’émissaire du ministère. Du côté des candidats, les épreuves se déroulent dans un climat de sérénité. Chacun espère décrocher une place parmi les 6 000 postes mis en compétition. Interrogée sur le déroulement des épreuves, Aminata Hélène Camara s’est montrée satisfaite des premières étapes du processus. « Le concours a bien débuté. Il y a eu l’accueil des candidats, leur installation et maintenant, nous sommes à l’étape des épreuves », a-t-elle indiqué. À l’issue du concours, les copies seront acheminées vers un centre sécurisé à Conakry pour y être corrigées à l’aide d’un correcteur optique. Les résultats seront ensuite mis à la disposition des candidats. Aboubacar Dramé, correspondant régional à Kindia +224 623 08 09 10 L’article Recrutement de 6 000 enseignants : forte mobilisation des candidats à Kindia est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Another Battle Between the Catholic Church and the Trump Administration
items.description: Several winters ago, a few weeks before Christmas, I went to confession. The parish close to work was hosting a reconciliation service, meant to prepare the faithful to celebrate the birth of Christ. A dozen or so priests were scattered across the cathedral. Penitents lined the aisles. Whispers of contrition and pardon filled the air. The Catholic Church counsels believers to seek confession regularly—at the very least, once a year. I hadn’t been back in a few. So in addition to feeling spiritually unmoored, I was worried about how the priest would react to hearing about my hiatus. But when I told him, he simply smiled and said, “Welcome back.” His response put me at ease then, and it helped change how I approach the sacrament now: less as a nerve-racking ordeal, more as a moment of mercy. Sacraments such as confession are central to Catholicism. Through them, the Church teaches that simple actions—having a conversation with a priest, eating bread and drinking wine—are, with grace, tangible encounters with God. For the past year, the Trump administration has been making it harder for Catholics at migrant-detention centers to have those encounters. The most recent example came to light this month, when the Archdiocese of St. Louis filed a federal lawsuit over the visitation policy at Saint Genevieve County Jail in eastern Missouri. According to the claim, the 10 priests who minister at the jail aren’t allowed to celebrate Mass. The suit also alleges that priests are permitted to visit migrant detainees just once a week, during a four-hour period, and that the jail’s “no contact” security policy lets the clergy speak with detainees only over the phone, through a glass partition. As a result, the approximately 150 migrants at the jail at a given time—most of whom are Catholic, according to the archdiocese—have been going without their religious needs for weeks. Since the middle of 2025, according to the lawsuit, Saint Genevieve has housed approximately 3,000 people. [ Read: The Catholic Church’s new schism ] This isn’t the first time that Catholic clergy have complained that the government is preventing them from ministering to detained migrants. Last year, the Florida detention facility known as “Alligator Alcatraz” kept priests from visiting or offering Mass to detainees for a month, until an agreement was reached between the Archdiocese of Miami and state authorities. In May, after a six-month legal fight, a Catholic nonprofit won a preliminary injunction to let Catholic priests celebrate Mass and administer sacraments at the Broadview ICE processing center outside Chicago. And the administration’s immigration crackdowns seem to be hurting the Church more broadly. Dioceses across the country have reported decreased Mass attendance among Spanish-speaking parishioners who fear detention. ICE has reportedly conducted raids near Catholic churches during Mass hours. The Department of Homeland Security has denied allegations of wrongdoing at Saint Genevieve. In a statement to multiple outlets, the agency said that the jail is not an ICE facility—although Saint Genevieve is listed as a detention facility on ICE’s website —and that it “ensures detainees are accommodated with religious services.” As described in the lawsuit, however, those accommodations disregard the religious significance of the Catholic sacraments. Consider confession. The suit claims that at Saint Genevieve, conversations between detainees and priests are not private, and the phone lines that they use to talk may be monitored. These policies may be in place for security reasons, but confession is meant to be a private exchange between penitent and priest, who acts in persona Christi —in the person of Christ. Confession is “one of the most intimate, profound acts that someone can do,” David Inczauskis, a Jesuit priest who ministers at the Broadview ICE facility, told me. He added, “To state very specifically the sins that they have committed and to ask humbly for pardon and for peace” requires a “level of vulnerability” that is “very high.” An even bigger problem comes up with the sacrament of the Eucharist, or Communion. The complaint includes an email from a deputy at the local sheriff’s office suggesting that priests “provide an unopened, individually wrapped Communion wafer” to a member of the detention center staff, who could then hand it to a detainee. This way of distributing the Eucharist would be “sacrilegious,” as Archbishop Mitchell Rozanski of St. Louis recently told Reuters . The Church teaches that the Eucharist is the “Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity” of Christ—not a symbol, but God’s real presence . For that reason, Inczauskis said, the Church distributes the Eucharist through either ordained ministers or specially trained laypeople. [ Read: The Catholic Church and the Trump administration are not getting along ] For much of the past quarter century, many conservative figures have taken up religious liberty as an essential cause. The Trump administration purported to continue these efforts when it established a commission last year meant to identify “emerging threats” to the exercise of faith. In June, the commission released a draft report claiming that “in recent years, Americans from all religious backgrounds have faced increasing persecution for their religious beliefs.” Some of the issues discussed in the report include rising anti-Semitism, how gender and sexuality is taught in schools, and conscience protections for health-care workers who object to participating in abortions or assisted suicides. The report said nothing about the administration’s migrant-detention practices. When the commission was announced, my colleague Elizabeth Bruenig wrote that “Christians shouldn’t conclude” that it would “necessarily defend their interests.” That warning seems prescient a year and a half later. At Alligator Alcatraz, Broadview, and Saint Genevieve, the Catholic Church has shown that it believes that detainee access to the sacraments matters deeply. Given the choice between restricting immigration and protecting the religious liberty of migrants, the administration, too, has demonstrated where its values lie.

items.title: The Flying Car Must Never Be Built
items.description: Elon Musk revealed, in a dramatic demonstration on Thursday night at SpaceX’s rocket-testing facility near Waco, Texas, a new “flying” Tesla Roadster prototype. The car hung upside down on a curved track, then performed aerial stunts—including jumping over a Tesla semi, Evel Knievel–style—using air-powered thrusters designed in collaboration with SpaceX. The demo was impressive despite Musk’s awkward manner, which in the context of a supposed literal flying car came off as nerdy charm. After revealing the car, Musk paraphrased a quote from Peter Thiel, his former PayPal partner: “We wanted flying cars, instead we got 140 characters.” The line, which was part of a 2011 “manifesto” published by Thiel’s venture-capital firm Founders Fund, was intended to indict the feeble ambition of the technology industry. Instead of solving big, important challenges, the world’s smarts—and money—had been devoted to small-potatoes social-internet start-ups such as Twitter. One obvious oddity of the line—which has since been removed from the manifesto —is that Founders Fund’s most important investment at the time was Facebook, a social-network platform. But another is the idea that anyone actually wanted a flying car for real. That ambition may never have represented an actual dream. Like a jet pack, a flying car represents not just the future but the idea of individual freedom delivered through technological conquest. Taken at face value, a flying car is not an impressive dream—or at least it hasn’t been since the Wright brothers more or less attained it. Automobiles have always moved on the ground by rolling via motor. The earliest practical airplanes also rolled until they flew (and hopefully landed again). An airplane is, in a way, merely a car with wings. [ Derek Thompson: Why flying cars are an impossible dream ] In 1917, Glenn Curtiss built literally that: His Curtiss Autoplane was an automobile with detachable wings and a propeller. It never really flew effectively, but the idea persisted. Waldo Waterman’s 1937 Arrowbile was more successful at flying, though it wasn’t commercially viable. Many more actual realizations of the supposed dream of flying cars appeared in the ensuing decades. The most famous might be the Taylor Aerocar, which was certified by the federal government in 1956 but was never mass-produced. Around that time, future-oriented science-factual magazines such as Popular Mechanics frequently rehearsed the vision of the personal aircraft. By then, cars were ordinary and mainstream in America, having displaced collective transportation such as trains and streetcars. The automobile had become a more abstract kind of vehicle, one that embraced and extended personal autonomy through the power to move, without effort, anywhere else—and to do it alone. But one thing still cramped the automobile’s capacity to deliver that freedom in full: roads. Cars needed them. The open road, of which America had a seemingly endless frontier, somehow was never enough. The best way around those roads was through the air above them; as Emmett Brown told Marty McFly inside one of fiction’s most memorable flying cars, “Roads? Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.” The stifling oppression of the ground, traversed at any speed, was also an old vexation. In 1923, Hugo Gernsback—sometimes called the father of science fiction thanks to his founding Amazing Stories , an early magazine devoted to the genre—imagined a gyroscopic Helicar that would release travelers from the tyranny of New York City’s newly car-congested streets. A few years later, in 1927, Fritz Lang’s film Metropolis colonized the city’s airspace with small flying vehicles. By 1962, the children’s cartoon The Jetsons had fused those precursors with mid-century Popular Mechanics populism, making the flying car a ubiquitous commuter vehicle. Over the decades, many attempts to engineer, manufacture, and market a flying car have been undertaken, though none has succeeded. In 1973, Henry Smolinski created the AVE Mizar by attaching Cessna wings to a Ford Pinto; it killed Smolinski during a failed test flight. From the 1960s until the company went dormant in the mid-2010s, Paul Moller made numerous attempts to develop the Skycar, a personal airplane that took off and landed vertically. Around that time, Terrafugia began promising a flying car called the Transition, which remained only a few years away for years—until the company shut down in 2021. “We enter production in 2028,” Musk said of the Tesla Roadster in this week’s Texas demo, before adding, “Actually.” By all appearances, the Roadster is not a flying car of the same sort as its real and fictional precursors. The vehicle’s air-fan system seems first and principally designed to give the car’s wheels better traction on the ground, which is part of why it can go so fast—it went from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second during the unveiling. (Rocket thrusters attached to the back of the thing also help.) The car does not fly so much as it performs aerial acrobatics such as barrel rolls and standing jumps. Those deeds were impressive as heck. The car certainly appeared to fly, if only for a moment, in the manner of a daredevil. Whether or not it can or is intended to fly in the manner of a traveler or commuter is not yet clear. Watching the Roadster do its thing—unpiloted, to make sure the demonstration didn’t “kill anyone,” as Musk put it—I imagined wealthy gearheads wreaking havoc via ill-fated jumps and spins on suburban blocks instead of salarymen conveying themselves to work and back. [ From the November 2026 issue: Choose your overlord ] Subdued by decades of failed automobile-airplane hybrids, and perhaps exhausted by Musk’s dubious intentions, some coverage of the Tesla demo has observed , rightly, that substantial regulatory hurdles await any vehicle that leaves the road and enters airspace. But bureaucratic red tape isn’t the main reason the flying-car dream hasn’t come to pass. Rather, it’s because the dream works better as fantasy than reality. When urban modernism began to feel cramped, the skies rising above it offered the possibility of new freedom. After the continent was settled, the roads that traversed it became new prisons from which airspace might allow escape. Once the individual freedom of the automobile became universal, and the roads clogged with thousands of varmints in the rat race, the blue sky above looked like liberty. George Jetson is a cog in the proverbial machine who rises above insignificance by flying to work unfazed, where he revels in the meaninglessness of his job pressing a button to make actual machine cogs. Even Thiel’s mention of the flying car was symbolic, a paradigmatic example of the kind of dream worth dreaming, not an actual one worth waking up to. Despite the Tesla Roadster’s truly spectacular capabilities, at least as a one-off demo, it fulfills the century-old flying-car ambition on a technicality—as a vehicle for a trick driver rather than a motorist aviator. Perhaps the dream this car truly realizes is not yours or mine, but Elon Musk’s: to claim to have delivered what a century of his forebears could not.

items.title: All the Comforts of Fall
items.description: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. There’s a lot to love about fall: the changing leaves, the crisp air, the return of cozy sweaters, and, of course, pumpkin-spice everything. As the days grow shorter and the weather cools, the season offers plenty of reasons to slow down and indulge in life’s little comforts. Although fall has its familiar rituals, there are always new ways to enjoy it. Maybe you’re looking for your next great read, a recipe to try on a chilly afternoon, or an excuse to spend more time outdoors before winter arrives. To help you get into the autumn spirit, explore some of our favorite Atlantic stories and recommendations for the season. Fall Favorites Six Books to Read by the Fire Each of these titles is a perfect companion while the days grow imperceptibly longer. By Amanda Parrish Morgan Read the article. Six Movies to Get You in the Fall Mood From cozy classics to unlikely favorites, The Atlantic ’s writers and editors share their seasonal picks. By Rafaela Jinich Read the article. How Starbucks Perfected Autumn The pumpkin spice latte has defined fall for 20 years. ( From 2023 ) By Ian Bogost Read the article. Still Curious? What the falling leaves taught Thoreau : His autumnal observations held a lesson for him in his final years, Jake Lundberg writes. No one knows how big pumpkins can get . A decade ago, the world’s heaviest pumpkin weighed 2,000 pounds. Now the 3,000-pound mark is within sight, Yasmin Tayag wrote in 2024. Other Diversions Can Elizabeth Holmes drop the act? The rise of the IRL influencer What three gene-therapy deaths have in common PS Courtesy of Lynn D. My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “We were lucky to head East before the storm because the foliage is incredibly colorful,” Lynn D. from Moretown, Vermont, shared. “This photo was taken from the Kancamagus Highway in New Hampshire.” We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. — Rafaela
